title: Real Vector Spaces and Complexification
---

Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $n$ and $\varphi \in \End(V)$. Since $\RR$ is not algebraically closed, $\varphi$ might have no eigenvalues, and then it cannot be put in triangular or Jordan form. Nevertheless, every real operator has an invariant subspace of dimension $1$ or $2$. The approach is to work over $\CC$, which is algebraically closed, by extending the scalars of $V$.

## <span class="num">7.10.1</span> The Complexification of a Real Vector Space

:::definition{7.10.1} Complexification
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\RR$. The ***complexification*** of $V$ is the set $V_{\CC} = V \times V$, whose elements $(v, w)$ we write as $v + iw$ ($v, w \in V$), with addition $$(v_1 + iw_1) + (v_2 + iw_2) = (v_1 + v_2) + i(w_1 + w_2)$$ and multiplication by complex scalars $$(a + ib)(v + iw) = (av - bw) + i(bv + aw), \qquad a, b \in \RR.$$ We identify $v \in V$ with $v + i0 \in V_{\CC}$. For $\mathbf{v} = v + iw$, the vectors $v = \operatorname{Re}(\mathbf{v})$ and $w = \operatorname{Im}(\mathbf{v})$ are its ***real*** and ***imaginary parts***.
:::

The scalar multiplication is what one gets by expanding $(a + ib)(v + iw)$ formally with $i^2 = -1$. Every element of $V_{\CC}$ is uniquely $v + iw$ with $v, w \in V$, so two elements are equal if and only if their real parts and their imaginary parts are equal. Note that $V \subseteq V_{\CC}$ is closed under addition and real scalars, but not under complex scalars: $i \cdot v = 0 + iv$.

:::proposition{7.10.2} $V_{\CC}$ is a complex vector space
With these operations, $V_{\CC}$ is a vector space over $\CC$. If $(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ is a basis of $V$ over $\RR$, then $(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ (that is, $(e_1 + i0, \ldots, e_n + i0)$) is a basis of $V_{\CC}$ over $\CC$. In particular, $\dim_{\CC} V_{\CC} = \dim_{\RR} V$.
:::

:::proof
Under addition, $V_{\CC} = V \times V$ is an abelian group. The scalar axioms are direct computations; for example, associativity: for $\alpha = a + ib$ and $\beta = c + id$, $$\begin{aligned}
\alpha\bigl(\beta(v + iw)\bigr) &= \alpha\bigl((cv - dw) + i(dv + cw)\bigr) \\
&= \bigl((ac - bd)v - (ad + bc)w\bigr) + i\bigl((ad + bc)v + (ac - bd)w\bigr) \\
&= (\alpha\beta)(v + iw),
\end{aligned}$$ since $\alpha\beta = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc)$. The distributive laws and $1 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$ are checked in the same way.

*Spanning:* if $v = \sum_j a_j e_j$ and $w = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $a_j, b_j \in \RR$, then $\sum_j (a_j + ib_j) e_j = \sum_j a_j e_j + i \sum_j b_j e_j = v + iw$.

*Independence:* if $\sum_j (a_j + ib_j) e_j = 0$, then comparing real and imaginary parts, $\sum_j a_j e_j = 0$ and $\sum_j b_j e_j = 0$, so all $a_j = b_j = 0$.
:::

:::example{7.10.3}
The complexification of $\RR^n$ is $\CC^n$: the element $x + iy$ of $(\RR^n)_{\CC}$, with $x, y \in \RR^n$, corresponds to the vector $(x_1 + iy_1, \ldots, x_n + iy_n) \in \CC^n$, and the operations match.
:::

:::definition{7.10.4} Complex conjugation
The ***complex conjugate*** of $\mathbf{v} = v + iw \in V_{\CC}$ is $\bar{\mathbf{v}} = v - iw$.
:::

Conjugation is additive, satisfies $\overline{\bar{\mathbf{v}}} = \mathbf{v}$, and is *conjugate-linear*: $\overline{\alpha \mathbf{v}} = \bar{\alpha}\, \bar{\mathbf{v}}$ for $\alpha \in \CC$. Indeed, for $\alpha = a + ib$, both $\overline{\alpha(v + iw)}$ and $(a - ib)(v - iw)$ equal $(av - bw) - i(bv + aw)$. A vector $\mathbf{v} \in V_{\CC}$ lies in $V$ if and only if $\bar{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}$, and $\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf{v}) = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{v} + \bar{\mathbf{v}})$, $\operatorname{Im}(\mathbf{v}) = \frac{1}{2i}(\mathbf{v} - \bar{\mathbf{v}})$.

## <span class="num">7.10.2</span> Complexifying Linear Maps

:::proposition{7.10.5} The complexification of a linear map
Let $\varphi : V \to W$ be an $\RR$-linear map between real vector spaces, and define $$\varphi_{\CC} : V_{\CC} \to W_{\CC}, \qquad \varphi_{\CC}(v + iw) = \varphi(v) + i\varphi(w).$$ Then:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $\varphi_{\CC}$ is $\CC$-linear, and it agrees with $\varphi$ on $V \subseteq V_{\CC}$.
2. $\varphi_{\CC}$ commutes with conjugation: $\varphi_{\CC}(\bar{\mathbf{v}}) = \overline{\varphi_{\CC}(\mathbf{v})}$.
3. $(\id_V)_{\CC} = \id_{V_{\CC}}$, and $(\psi \circ \varphi)_{\CC} = \psi_{\CC} \circ \varphi_{\CC}$ for every $\RR$-linear $\psi : W \to U$.
4. If $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional with bases $\mcB$ and $\mcC$, then $\mcM(\varphi_{\CC}, \mcB, \mcC) = \mcM(\varphi, \mcB, \mcC)$, where $\mcB$ and $\mcC$ are regarded as complex bases of $V_{\CC}$ and $W_{\CC}$ (Proposition [7.10.2](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#proposition-7-10-2)). In particular, for an operator $\varphi \in \End(V)$, $\chi_{\varphi_{\CC}} = \chi_\varphi$, a polynomial with real coefficients.
:::

:::proof
(a) Additivity is clear. For $a, b \in \RR$, $$\begin{aligned}
\varphi_{\CC}\bigl((a + ib)(v + iw)\bigr) &= \varphi_{\CC}\bigl((av - bw) + i(bv + aw)\bigr) \\
&= \bigl(a\varphi(v) - b\varphi(w)\bigr) + i\bigl(b\varphi(v) + a\varphi(w)\bigr),
\end{aligned}$$ which is $(a + ib)\bigl(\varphi(v) + i\varphi(w)\bigr)$. And $\varphi_{\CC}(v + i0) = \varphi(v) + i0$.

(b) $\varphi_{\CC}(v - iw) = \varphi(v) - i\varphi(w) = \overline{\varphi(v) + i\varphi(w)}$.

(c) Clearly $(\id_V)_{\CC}(v + iw) = v + iw$, and $(\psi \circ \varphi)_{\CC}(v + iw) = \psi(\varphi(v)) + i\psi(\varphi(w)) = \psi_{\CC}\bigl(\varphi(v) + i\varphi(w)\bigr) = \psi_{\CC}(\varphi_{\CC}(v + iw))$.

(d) If $\mcB = (e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ and $\mcC = (f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, then $\varphi_{\CC}(e_j) = \varphi(e_j) = \sum_i a_{ij} f_i$, so the $j$-th columns of the two matrices agree. The characteristic polynomial of an operator is computed from its matrix.
:::

:::note
Part (c) says that $V \mapsto V_{\CC}$, $\varphi \mapsto \varphi_{\CC}$ is a functor from real to complex vector spaces, in the language of Chapter 8 (Example [8.2.4](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#example-8-2-4)).
:::

Now let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ be an operator on a finite-dimensional real space $V$. Then $\varphi_{\CC}$ is an operator on a complex vector space, so it is guaranteed to have an eigenvector if $V \neq \{0\}$ (and it has generalized eigenspaces and a Jordan form). Its eigenvectors tell us about $\varphi$.

:::proposition{7.10.6} Eigenvectors of the complexification
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$, where $V$ is a real vector space, and let $\mathbf{v} = v + iw$ be an eigenvector of $\varphi_{\CC}$ with eigenvalue $\lambda \in \CC$.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. If $\lambda \in \RR$, then $v$ and $w$ lie in $E(\lambda, \varphi)$, and at least one of them is nonzero; so $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\varphi$. Conversely, every eigenvalue of $\varphi$ is an eigenvalue of $\varphi_{\CC}$. Thus the real eigenvalues of $\varphi_{\CC}$ are exactly the eigenvalues of $\varphi$.
2. If $\lambda = a + ib$ with $b \neq 0$, then $\bar{\mathbf{v}}$ is an eigenvector of $\varphi_{\CC}$ with eigenvalue $\bar{\lambda}$; the vectors $v, w \in V$ are linearly independent; and $U = \operatorname{Span}_{\RR}(v, w)$ is a two-dimensional $\varphi$-invariant subspace of $V$, with $$\varphi(v) = av - bw, \quad \varphi(w) = bv + aw, \qquad \mcM\bigl(\varphi|_U, (v, w)\bigr) = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \end{pmatrix}.$$
:::

:::proof
In both cases, $\varphi_{\CC}(\mathbf{v}) = \varphi(v) + i\varphi(w)$ and $\lambda\mathbf{v} = (a + ib)(v + iw) = (av - bw) + i(bv + aw)$, where $\lambda = a + ib$. Comparing real and imaginary parts, $$\varphi(v) = av - bw, \qquad \varphi(w) = bv + aw.$$

(a) If $b = 0$, this says $\varphi(v) = av$ and $\varphi(w) = aw$, and $v, w$ are not both zero because $\mathbf{v} \neq 0$. Conversely, an eigenvector $v \in V$ of $\varphi$ is an eigenvector of $\varphi_{\CC}$ with the same eigenvalue, by Proposition [7.10.5](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#proposition-7-10-5)(a).

(b) By Proposition [7.10.5](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#proposition-7-10-5)(b), $\varphi_{\CC}(\bar{\mathbf{v}}) = \overline{\lambda\mathbf{v}} = \bar{\lambda}\bar{\mathbf{v}}$, and $\bar{\mathbf{v}} \neq 0$. Since $\lambda \neq \bar{\lambda}$, the eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}$ are linearly independent over $\CC$ (Theorem [7.4.4](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#theorem-7-4-4)). As $v = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{v} + \bar{\mathbf{v}})$ and $w = \frac{1}{2i}(\mathbf{v} - \bar{\mathbf{v}})$, and conversely $\mathbf{v} = v + iw$, $\bar{\mathbf{v}} = v - iw$, the complex spans of $(v, w)$ and of $(\mathbf{v}, \bar{\mathbf{v}})$ coincide and are two-dimensional; so $v, w$ are linearly independent over $\CC$, and in particular over $\RR$. The displayed formulas show $\varphi(U) \subseteq U$, and the columns of the matrix are the coordinates of $\varphi(v) = a \cdot v + (-b) \cdot w$ and $\varphi(w) = b \cdot v + a \cdot w$.
:::

:::theorem{7.10.7} Invariant subspaces of real operators
Every operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional real vector space has an invariant subspace of dimension $1$ or $2$.
:::

:::proof
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ with $V \neq \{0\}$ finite-dimensional over $\RR$. Then $V_{\CC}$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space, and $\CC$ is algebraically closed (the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, Chapter 4), so $\varphi_{\CC}$ has an eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ (Theorem [7.5.1](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-1)). If its eigenvalue is real, Proposition [7.10.6](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#proposition-7-10-6)(a) gives an eigenvector of $\varphi$, which spans a one-dimensional invariant subspace. Otherwise, Proposition [7.10.6](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#proposition-7-10-6)(b) gives a two-dimensional invariant subspace.
:::

:::example{7.10.8} The rotation, revisited
Let $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ act on $\RR^2$. It has no eigenvalues, but its complexification (the same matrix acting on $\CC^2$) has the eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = (1, -i)^t$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = i$: indeed $R\mathbf{v} = (i, 1)^t = i\,(1, -i)^t$. Here $v = \operatorname{Re}(\mathbf{v}) = (1, 0)^t$, $w = \operatorname{Im}(\mathbf{v}) = (0, -1)^t$, $a = 0$ and $b = 1$. The formulas of Proposition [7.10.6](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#proposition-7-10-6) say $Rv = -w = (0, 1)^t$ and $Rw = v = (1, 0)^t$, which is correct, and $U = \RR^2$ with matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$ in the basis $(v, w)$. The conjugate $\bar{\mathbf{v}} = (1, i)^t$ is the eigenvector for $\bar{\lambda} = -i$.
:::

:::note
Since $\chi_{\varphi_{\CC}} = \chi_\varphi$ has real coefficients, its non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, matching the pairing $\mathbf{v} \leftrightarrow \bar{\mathbf{v}}$ of eigenvectors. A real eigenvalue of $\varphi_{\CC}$ contributes eigenvectors of $\varphi$ itself, while each pair $\lambda, \bar{\lambda}$ of non-real eigenvalues contributes a two-dimensional invariant subspace on which $\varphi$ acts by a matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \end{psmallmatrix}$, a rotation combined with a scaling. Continuing by induction with the induced operator on $V/U$ (Proposition [7.3.5](/notes/math-55a/7-3-invariant-subspaces#proposition-7-3-5)), as in the proof of Theorem [7.5.2](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-2), one can put every real operator in block upper-triangular form with diagonal blocks of size $1$ or $2$. Complexification returns in Chapter 9, for operators on real inner product spaces, and in Chapter 16, for real representations.
:::
